Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 5 periods = 200 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 20min

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Picture Reading (pp.1–2): guided picture walk through all four illustrations.

periods.activity_title: Picture Walk — Duck, Hen and the Village Fair
materials: Pointer or finger for picture sequencing

time_bands.activity: Teacher walks students through the four illustrations one by one, asking what they see in each picture — who is there, where they are going, what is happening at the stream.
Picture Reading — "guided picture walk through all four illustrations." Teacher reads aloud the speech-bubble dialogue from the textbook as each character speaks, keeping pace with the pictures.
Students look at the pictures again in pairs and take turns pointing to each scene and saying in one sentence what is happening — the duck inviting the hen, the journey, the stream, the crossing.
Whole class shares: teacher asks, "Which picture surprised you most?" Students respond briefly in one sentence each. Teacher affirms and links all four pictures as one connected story.

periods.teacher_notes: The four pictures carry the whole story without needing words first — let observation lead before dialogue is introduced. A common pitfall is moving too quickly past the stream picture; pause here and let students notice the ducklings carrying the chicks, because that detail drives all the discussion in later work.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Picture Reading (pp.1–2): shared reading of speech-bubble dialogue with character roles.

periods.activity_title: Re-reading the Dialogue Aloud — What the Characters Say

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the story by pointing to each picture in the textbook and naming the key event — the invitation, the journey, the stream problem, and the crossing — so the speech bubbles have context.
Shared reading of the dialogue from Textbook pp. 1–2. Teacher reads the duck's lines, the class reads the hen's lines together, then roles swap. Each line is read twice for fluency.

Students read the full dialogue in pairs, one taking the duck's voice and the other the hen's. Teacher circulates, supporting accurate phrasing — especially "I have a plan" — as a natural spoken sentence.
Two volunteer pairs read the dialogue to the class. Teacher draws attention to how the duck sounds calm and reassuring and the hen sounds worried — brief discussion of how mood shows through words.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored the pictures in the previous picture-walk, students now have the full visual story in mind, which makes reading the speech bubbles meaningful rather than mechanical. Watch for students who read "I cannot swim" flatly — prompt them to read it the way a worried hen might really say it.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Now discuss with your friends (p.3): guided conversation on all five discussion questions.

periods.activity_title: Now Discuss — Friends, Help, and the Stream
materials: Chalkboard or whiteboard for the closing shared sentence

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the picture on the page showing the stream crossing and asks students to look quietly for a moment. Without prompting, students say in one word what they see — builds readiness for the questions that follow.

Now discuss with your friends (p.3) — "guided conversation on all five discussion questions." Teacher poses each question one at a time, gives students a moment to think, then invites two or three voices per question. Questions 1–3 focus on what happened in the story.

Questions 4 and 5 invite students to share from their own lives — a time they helped a friend and whether it felt good. Pairs talk first, then the class shares one story. Teacher listens and responds warmly without correcting personal experiences.

Whole class closes by agreeing on one sentence that sums up the duck's plan — teacher writes it on the board as students dictate. This shared sentence anchors the story's main idea in the students' own words.

periods.teacher_notes: The five questions move deliberately from observation (counting the ducklings and chicks) through inference (how do we know they are friends?) to personal reflection (have you helped a friend?). Keep Question 1 quick and factual so more time is available for Questions 4 and 5, where the richer discussion lives.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Now discuss with your friends (p.3): oral retelling of the story using the four pictures as prompts.

periods.activity_title: Retelling the Story — The Duck and Hen's Journey

time_bands.activity: Teacher models a short retelling of the picture story — three or four sentences spoken aloud while pointing to the textbook pictures — to show students what a story retell sounds like: beginning, middle, and what happened at the stream.

Students practise retelling in pairs, each partner retelling from a different picture. One student begins with the duck's invitation; the partner continues with the stream and the crossing. Textbook remains open for reference.

Three or four volunteers retell the whole story to the class without looking at the pictures. Class listens and gives a quiet thumbs-up when the teller mentions the ducklings carrying the chicks — the key event.

Teacher asks: "What is the most important thing the duck did for the hen?" Students respond in one sentence. Teacher collects two or three answers and links them to the idea that each friend's strength helps the other.

periods.teacher_notes: Retelling after the guided conversation about friendship and help means students have already thought about what matters in the story. A common difficulty is that students retell only the ending — gently prompt them to start from the invitation so the sequence stays intact.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Match the following animals with their young ones (p.3): matching animal names to their young-one vocabulary.

periods.activity_title: Animals and Their Young — Matching Word Play
materials: Chalkboard or whiteboard for the two scrambled columns

time_bands.activity: Teacher points to the duck and the hen in the textbook pictures and says their young ones' names — duckling, chick — asking students to repeat. Then adds cow, cat, and dog, and elicits any young-one names students already know.

Match the following animals with their young ones (p.3) — "matching animal names to their young-one vocabulary." Teacher writes the five animals and five young-one words on the board in two scrambled columns. Class calls out matches one at a time as teacher draws lines.

Students complete the matching task in their textbooks individually. Teacher circulates and prompts gently where a student is uncertain — for example, asking "What do we call a baby cat?" rather than giving the answer directly.

Quick whole-class check: teacher calls an animal name, students call back the young one's name together. Then reverse — teacher says the young one, students say the parent animal. Pairs finish with a quick riddle: "I am soft and I say mew — what is my mother called?"

periods.teacher_notes: The five animal pairs in the matching task extend the duck–hen vocabulary students encountered in the picture story into a small structured set. Watch for confusion between puppy and kitten — both are small and fluffy; linking kitten firmly to the word cat helps.

items.source_context: Four-picture sequence of duck and hen travelling to a fair, crossing a stream with young ones.
items.item_stem:
Look at the picture story on Textbook pages 1–2. The events below are jumbled. Choose the option that puts them in the correct order.
1. The ducklings carry the chicks across the stream.
2. The duck invites the hen to the village fair.
3. The hen says she cannot swim.
4. They all reach the stream.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students who choose this may think the crossing happened before the journey began, showing they have not followed the picture sequence.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals the student has the beginning right but placed the hen's worry before the group reaches the stream — a small but meaningful sequencing slip.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student started from the stream picture and worked backwards, missing the story's opening invitation entirely.

items.source_lo: Student observes and sequences visual narrative events using a picture story as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four-picture sequence of duck and hen travelling to a fair, crossing a stream with young ones.
items.item_stem: Look at the picture on Textbook page 2 that shows the group at the stream. The hen says, "I cannot swim. How shall we cross the stream?" How does the duck solve this problem? Write one or two sentences in your own words.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The duck uses her plan of having the ducklings swim across with the chicks sitting on their backs, so all of them cross the stream safely.

items.source_lo: Student infers character relationships and narrates story events drawing on personal experience using a picture dialogue as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Duck and hen's friendship, the stream problem, ducklings carrying chicks; personal help experiences.
items.item_stem:
Read the line below from the story:
"Come dear hen, let us go to the village fair."
Who says this, and what does it tell us about how this character feels about the hen?

options.text: The duck is being unfriendly in this line.
The duck says this line to the hen.
The duck wants to go to the fair alone.
The word "dear" shows the duck cares about the hen.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is true — the duck speaks this line. Statement 2 is false — the duck is being warm and friendly. Statement 3 is false — the duck invites the hen to come along. Statement 4 is true — "dear" is a word used for someone we care about.

items.source_lo: Student infers character relationships and narrates story events drawing on personal experience using a picture dialogue as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Duck and hen's friendship, the stream problem, ducklings carrying chicks; personal help experiences.
items.item_stem: Think about the duck and the hen in the picture story. The duck says, "I have a plan," when the hen is worried about crossing the stream. Tell your class: Has a friend ever helped YOU when you had a problem? What did your friend do, and how did it make you feel?

expected_elements: Names a real or believable problem faced.
Describes what the friend did to help.
Shares a feeling — happy, relieved, grateful.

items.item_stem: In the picture story, the hen brings her chicks and the duck brings her ducklings to the village fair. Choose ONE of these young-one words — chick, duckling, calf, kitten, or puppy — and say one sentence about that young animal. Your sentence must say what that young animal's parent is called.

expected_elements: Names a young-one word from the chapter.
